specPoints.text: practical: investigate the magnetic field pattern for a permanent bar magnet and between two bar magnets

primer.text: This practical draws the invisible: a plotting compass, a pencil and a chain of dots turn a bar magnet's field into a visible map. The method steps the compass tail-to-dot, the analysis reads crowding as strength and straightness as uniformity, and the honest error analysis is part of the mark scheme.

lessons.title: Aim and equipment of the field-mapping practical
lessons.opening: The investigation maps two field patterns on paper: the field of one permanent bar magnet, and the field in the region between two bar magnets. The kit is deliberately minimal — bar magnets, a plotting compass, paper and a pencil — because the compass itself is the sensor.
keyPoints: The aim is to plot the field patterns for one bar magnet and for the gap between two of them.
A plotting compass is the sensor: its needle aligns with the local field line direction.
Paper, pencil and a ruler record each needle direction as a small arrow.
Two bar magnets and a support setup extend the map to the between-magnet region.
Every arrow is drawn where the compass sits, so the pattern builds point by point.

low.restatement: Put a magnet on the paper, place the compass near one pole, and draw a tiny arrow showing where the needle points. Move the compass a little further along the arrow and repeat — the arrows join up into the field lines.
low.analogy: It is like mapping a wind field with a tiny weathervane: record its direction at each spot, then connect the spots into streamlines.
low.examPointer: Quote the aim in the question's own terms — the pattern FOR a bar magnet AND between two bar magnets — quoting only one half drops a mark.

medium.restatement: The design treats the compass needle as a north-pole test dipole: at each position the needle's north end is pushed along the local field direction, so the marked arrow is a tangent to the field line through that point. Chaining tangent-to-tangent steps reconstructs the full line without ever measuring field strength directly.
medium.analogy: Each compass reading is one frame of a time-lapse: no single frame shows the path, but playing them in order reveals the whole trajectory.
medium.examPointer: If asked why the compass is small, answer: a small needle samples the direction at a point instead of averaging the field across a large area.

check.stem: What is the aim of this field-mapping investigation?

options.text: to plot the field pattern for a bar magnet and between two bar magnets
options.explanation: Both regions — single magnet and the two-magnet gap — are the targets.

options.text: to measure the strength of Earth's magnetic field
options.explanation: Earth's field is a nuisance here, not the measurement.

options.text: to find which magnet is strongest
options.explanation: No strength comparison is made — only the pattern is mapped.

options.text: to induce magnetism in the compass needle
options.explanation: The needle is the sensor, not the sample.

check.stem: Which instrument shows the direction of the field at a point?

options.text: a small plotting compass
options.explanation: Its needle aligns with the local field line.

options.text: a stopwatch
options.explanation: Nothing here is timed.

options.text: a voltmeter
options.explanation: No electrical quantity is measured in this practical.

options.text: a force meter
options.explanation: Forces are not measured — directions are plotted.

check.stem: Why must each compass arrow be drawn exactly where the compass sits?

options.text: the arrow is the tangent to the field line at that point
options.explanation: Each reading samples one local direction of the field.

options.text: so the compass does not demagnetise the magnets
options.explanation: The compass is far too weak to demagnetise the magnets.

options.text: because the field changes while you watch
options.explanation: A static magnet's field is steady.

options.text: to keep the paper flat
options.explanation: Drawing position has nothing to do with paper flatness.

check.stem: A student maps with a large compass nearly as long as the magnet. Why is this poor design?

options.text: a long needle averages the field over many points instead of sampling one
options.explanation: Direction-at-a-point needs a small sensor.

options.text: large compasses lose their magnetism quickly
options.explanation: Size does not change the needle's magnetisation.

options.text: the needle would point at the ceiling
options.explanation: Nothing in the setup gives a vertical force.

options.text: large compasses only work near the poles
options.explanation: A compass works anywhere the field is strong enough.

check.stem: Which list of kit is sufficient: bar magnets, plotting compass, paper, pencil?

options.text: bar magnets, plotting compass, paper, pencil
options.explanation: These four cover source, sensor, canvas and record.

options.text: iron filings, water bath, thermometer
options.explanation: That kit belongs to other practicals entirely.

options.text: ammeter, wires, power supply
options.explanation: No circuit is involved in this magnetic-field practical.

options.text: stopwatch and ticker tape
options.explanation: Nothing moves in a measurable time way here.

check.stem: State the two field patterns this practical is asked to plot.
check.modelAnswer: The field pattern for a single permanent bar magnet, and the field pattern in the region between two bar magnets.

check.stem: State the role of the plotting compass in the method.
check.modelAnswer: The compass needle aligns with the local field, so its direction marks the field line direction at that point.

check.stem: Explain why the plotted arrows from many compass positions join into smooth curves.
check.modelAnswer: Each arrow is the local field direction, and the field direction changes smoothly from point to point. Stepping the compass along the previous arrow keeps sampling the next tangent, so the chain of arrows traces the continuous curve that is the field line.

check.stem: A student's map of a single bar magnet shows arrows pointing INTO the north pole. What has gone wrong and how is it fixed?
check.modelAnswer: The arrows are reversed: field lines leave the north pole, so the needle's north end points away from it. The student drew the SOUTH end of the needle instead — replotting with the arrow along the needle's marked north end fixes the map.

lessons.title: Method: stepping the compass around the magnets
lessons.opening: The method is a deliberate walk: place the compass near a pole, mark the needle's two ends with dots, slide the compass so its tail sits on the last dot, and repeat. The dot-chain grows into a field line, and enough chains make the whole pattern.
keyPoints: Place the magnet on paper and the compass near one pole to start.
Mark dots at both ends of the needle, then move the compass so its tail end sits on the far dot.
Repeating the dot-marking builds a chain of dots along one field line.
Join the dots with a smooth curve and add an arrow showing the direction away from the north pole.
Repeat from several starting points to reveal the complete pattern.

low.restatement: Dot the needle ends, leapfrog the compass to the next dot, dot again. Join the dots into a curve, arrow it away from the north pole, and start a new chain somewhere else on the paper.
low.analogy: It is like hopping along a path in the dark: each hop lands where the last heading pointed, and the footprints trace the route.
low.examPointer: The mark scheme wants 'mark the needle positions' and 'join the dots' — quote both steps in method answers.

medium.restatement: Leapfrogging keeps every new reading tangent to the same field line: the compass tail on the last dot means the next needle direction continues the previous heading, so small alignment errors do not accumulate into a different line. Starting chains from many points around the pole fills in the density picture as well as the direction picture.
medium.analogy: A relay runner hands over exactly at the baton mark — each leg continues the same route instead of drifting to a new one.
medium.examPointer: For the between-two-magnets map, start chains across the whole gap: the mid-region lines come out straight and parallel — evidence of uniformity.

check.stem: What is done with the compass after marking its needle-end dots?

options.text: it is moved so its tail sits on the far dot, then new dots are marked
options.explanation: The leapfrog step extends the dot-chain along one line.

options.text: it is lifted away to check the reading again
options.explanation: Lifting it away loses the tangent continuation.

options.text: it is swapped for iron filings
options.explanation: Filings are a different mapping method entirely.

options.text: it is turned around to point backwards
options.explanation: The needle aligns with the field by itself; no manual turning.

check.stem: Why start new dot-chains from several different points near the magnet?

options.text: different starting points follow different field lines, filling in the pattern
options.explanation: One chain is one line; the pattern needs many.

options.text: to check the compass battery
options.explanation: A plotting compass has no battery.

options.text: because one reading is too quick to time
options.explanation: Nothing is timed in this practical.

options.text: to make the magnet lose strength slowly
options.explanation: Mapping does not weaken the magnet.

check.stem: In which direction is the arrow drawn on a finished dot-chain?

options.text: away from the magnet's north pole, along the chain
options.explanation: Field-line arrows leave north poles.

options.text: into the north pole
options.explanation: That reverses the field-line convention.

options.text: always towards the paper edge
options.explanation: Arrows follow the field, not the paper geometry.

options.text: no arrow is drawn on field lines
options.explanation: Direction arrows are essential to the map.

check.stem: The dot-chain wobbles off the smooth curve after many leapfrog steps. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: small misalignments of the compass accumulate step by step
options.explanation: Each step adds a little angle error to the chain.

options.text: the magnet reversed its poles during the mapping
options.explanation: Permanent magnets do not flip poles mid-practical.

options.text: the pencil lines were too dark
options.explanation: Ink darkness cannot bend a field line.

options.text: the compass needle lost its magnetism
options.explanation: A dead needle gives random readings, not a slow wobble.

check.stem: When mapping between two magnets with opposite poles facing, what should the central chains show?

options.text: straight, parallel, equally spaced lines across the gap
options.explanation: The central gap field is uniform.

options.text: circles centred on the gap
options.explanation: Circles belong to current-carrying wires.

options.text: lines that never enter the gap
options.explanation: The gap is exactly where the field lines run.

options.text: randomly crossing curves
options.explanation: Field lines never cross anywhere.

check.stem: State the leapfrog rule of the dot method.
check.modelAnswer: Move the compass so its tail end sits on the last marked dot before marking the next pair of dots.

check.stem: State how a completed dot-chain is turned into a field line.
check.modelAnswer: Join the dots with a smooth curve and add an arrowhead pointing away from the north pole.

check.stem: Explain why the leapfrogging keeps the chain on ONE field line instead of wandering onto a neighbour.
check.modelAnswer: Placing the compass tail on the previous dot makes the next reading continue the direction recorded there, so each new dot is a small step along the same tangent. The chain therefore follows the smooth change of direction of one field line, rather than jumping to a neighbouring line where the field points elsewhere.

check.stem: A class maps the two-magnet gap and their central chains are curved, not straight. Suggest the magnet fault that best explains it.
check.modelAnswer: The most likely fault is that the facing poles are not opposite — one magnet is turned so like poles face, giving a neutral-point pattern instead of a uniform gap. Swapping one magnet round so opposite poles face should straighten the central chains into parallel, equally spaced lines.

lessons.title: Analysis: reading the mapped patterns
lessons.opening: The finished map is read twice: once for direction — arrows leaving north, entering south — and once for strength, where crowded lines mean a strong field. Between two magnets the straight, evenly spaced central lines are the evidence for a uniform field, and the wobbly edge chains are the honest error analysis.
keyPoints: Arrows on every curve run away from the north pole and into the south pole.
Lines crowd together at the poles, showing the strongest field regions.
Between opposite poles the central lines are straight, parallel and equally spaced — a uniform field.
Compass misalignment accumulates along a chain, so chains are restarted often.
Earth's field slightly bends the outer chains — a disclosed limitation of the method.

low.restatement: Look at the map: arrows out of the north end, into the south end; lines bunched at the poles; and, between two magnets, a neat ladder of straight lines in the middle. Bunching means strong, spacing means uniform.
low.analogy: Reading the map is like reading traffic flow on a road plan: arrow direction gives the way, lane crowding gives the congestion.
low.examPointer: Use the phrase 'uniform field' with its drawing evidence — straight, parallel, equally spaced — analysis marks live on that pairing.

medium.restatement: The dot-chain method samples direction only, so strength is inferred from chain density — more chains per unit area where the field is strong. Systematic bends from Earth's field appear at the map's edges where the magnet's field weakens, and chain-accumulated angle error shows as wobbling curves; both are disclosed rather than smoothed away.
medium.analogy: The map is a pencil sketch of the field: good in the middle where the field is bold, shakier at the edges where the subject fades.
medium.examPointer: Evaluation answers earn credit for NAMED improvements: restart chains frequently, work away from steel desks, and keep phones with magnets out of the way.

check.stem: What does the crowding of lines near a pole tell you?

options.text: the field is strongest there
options.explanation: Dense chains mean a strong field.

options.text: the field is weakest there
options.explanation: It is the opposite: spacing widens as the field weakens.

options.text: the magnet is warm there
options.explanation: Temperature plays no role in the map.

options.text: the compass was moved too slowly
options.explanation: Mapping speed does not change the pattern.

check.stem: Which feature of the two-magnet map is the evidence for a uniform field?

options.text: straight, parallel, equally spaced central lines
options.explanation: That drawing pattern is the uniform-field signature.

options.text: curved lines at the paper edge
options.explanation: Edge curves are fringing and Earth-field effects.

options.text: the number of magnets used
options.explanation: The pattern, not the count, is the evidence.

options.text: arrows pointing both ways on one line
options.explanation: Each line carries one direction only.

check.stem: Why do the outer chains of the single-magnet map bend slightly away from the ideal picture?

options.text: Earth's magnetic field competes with the weak outer field of the magnet
options.explanation: Far from the poles the magnet's field is comparable to Earth's.

options.text: the pencil was blunt
options.explanation: Drawing quality cannot bend a compass needle.

options.text: the magnet's field changes over minutes
options.explanation: A permanent magnet's field is steady during the practical.

options.text: the compass needle is too light
options.explanation: Needle mass does not bend the alignment.

check.stem: A student's central chains in the two-magnet gap are straight but NOT parallel, fanning out slightly. What does the fan shape indicate?

options.text: the field in that region is not uniform
options.explanation: Uniformity requires parallel lines, not just straight ones.

options.text: the field there is uniform but weak
options.explanation: Fanning means the direction varies — non-uniform.

options.text: the magnets are too strong
options.explanation: Strength changes spacing, not straightness.

options.text: the paper was moved during plotting
options.explanation: Moving paper shifts the whole map, not a selective fan.

check.stem: Which improvement most reduces chain wobble?

options.text: restarting chains from a fresh compass placement every few steps
options.explanation: Fresh starts stop angle errors accumulating.

options.text: using a longer compass
options.explanation: Longer needles average over more field, worsening point sampling.

options.text: plotting faster
options.explanation: Speed adds carelessness, not accuracy.

options.text: using a thicker pencil
options.explanation: Line thickness is cosmetic here.

check.stem: State two features read from the single-magnet map.
check.modelAnswer: Arrows leave the north pole and enter the south pole, and the lines crowd together near the poles where the field is strongest.

check.stem: State the drawing signature of the uniform field between opposite poles.
check.modelAnswer: The central lines are straight, parallel and equally spaced.

check.stem: Explain why chains plotted far from the magnet are the least trustworthy part of the map.
check.modelAnswer: Far from the poles the magnet's field is weak, so Earth's magnetic field is a comparable competitor: the needle aligns with the resultant of the two rather than with the magnet's field alone. The compass also responds to any nearby steel or magnets in the room, so weak-field chains bend for reasons that have nothing to do with the magnet being mapped.

check.stem: Two students map the same magnet; one works on a steel desk, the other on a wooden bench. Their maps differ most in the outer chains. Explain which map to trust and why.
check.modelAnswer: Trust the wooden-bench map. Steel is a magnetic material, so the desk both distorts the magnet's outer field and induces its own poles, dragging nearby chains. The wooden bench adds no magnetic interference, so its outer chains reflect the magnet's true field.

glossary.definition: A small magnetic compass used to find the direction of a magnetic field at a point.
The sequence of needle-end dots that traces one field line on the map.
A field with the same strength and direction at every point, drawn as straight parallel equally spaced lines.
